transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Well, honestly, my boss kind of sent me here... or, well, strongly suggested I come in, because things have just gotten completely out of hand at my job. I do general maintenance and repair—you know, fixing things around the facility, a little plumbing, drywall, whatever breaks down on any given day. But the problem is... I just keep forgetting things. 

And not just little things, but really important stuff. Like, I’ll have scheduled callbacks with vendors or contractors, and they just completely slip my mind. Or I'll get a stack of work orders, and I swear I look at them and plan to do them, but then someone stops me in the hall and I just forget they even exist. Even just basic follow-ups! Like, I’ll fix a leaky pipe and promise the person I’ll swing back by in the afternoon to make sure it’s holding up, and I just... I completely blank on it. I don't mean to, I just do. 

And now all these missed tickets and forgotten promises have piled up so much that my supervisor actually had to pull me into the office for a formal sit-down. Which is just humiliating, you know? I'm 49, I work hard, I know how to fix things. But there's a lead position opening up soon, and they basically told me they had to send me here to get this sorted out immediately before I completely lose my shot at moving up. I just don't know why my brain is acting like a sieve lately, but I really need to get it under control.
Were you having similar attention or forgetfulness problems as a child, before age 12?

Oh, gosh... yeah. Actually, yes. It’s funny you ask about that, because I've been trying to tell myself lately that this is all just the stress of the job, you know? Like maybe the volume of tickets is just too high, or I'm just getting older and tired. But if I'm being completely honest with myself... no, it's not new. I remember being exactly this way way back in grade school. I mean, long, long before any of this current job pressure or worrying about getting a lead position. 

My mom actually kept a bunch of my old report cards in this big plastic tub, and I remember looking through them a while back. Every single one of them, from first grade all the way up, told the exact same story. The teachers would always write the same notes—and they’d tell my parents this at the parent-teacher conferences too—they'd say I was a really bright girl, that I had all this potential and I was smart. But then there was always the "but." 

It was always, "but she constantly misplaces her papers." And it was true! I would sit there and do my homework at the kitchen table, put it right in my folder, and somehow by the time I got to my desk the next morning, it had just vanished into thin air. I was always losing my assignments. And if the teacher stood up at the chalkboard and gave us instructions for a project? Forget it. If it was more than one step, I'd hear the first part, and then my brain would just sort of check out and I'd miss whole parts of the directions. I'd be looking around the room seeing everyone else working and I'd have to whisper to the kid next to me to figure out what we were even supposed to be doing. 

The teachers always had to hover over me or give me special reminders just to get me to finish my regular classwork. And I wasn't a bad kid, you know? I wasn't throwing spitballs or causing trouble in the back of the room, I just... I couldn't keep a thought in my head to save my life, even back then. So, yeah, this has definitely been trailing me around since I was a little kid. It's just that now it's about to cost me my livelihood instead of just a grade on a spelling test.
